<description>
{
 "summary": "Makes legacy BDB to SQLite wallet migration handle failures gracefully instead of aborting on assertions. MakeSQLiteDatabase is updated to track and clean up files and directories created during an unsuccessful open or verify attempt. MigrateToSQLite now stages records into a temporary database inside a migration directory, swapping the new database into place and deleting the legacy database only after all records are committed.",
 "problem": "When migrating a BDB wallet to SQLite, MigrateToSQLite deletes the existing wallet file before creating the new SQLite database and calls assert on database creation and record commits. If database creation fails\u2014such as on CIFS/SMB or NFS mounts that do not support SQLite file locking, or due to insufficient disk space or permission errors\u2014the node crashes with an assertion failure and leaves behind an empty wallet file.",
 "evidence": [
  "PR description reports a node abort (Assertion 'new_db' failed) when attempting to migrate a wallet on a CIFS mount where fcntl F_SETLK fails with EACCES",
  "Diff in src/wallet/wallet.cpp removes assert(new_db), assert(began), and assert(committed) in MigrateToSQLite and replaces them with transactional rollback, cleanup, and user-facing error messages"

<category name="wallet" title="Wallet">
## Covers

The bitcoind wallet: key and descriptor management, transaction creation
and coin selection, PSBT handling, wallet database (SQLite, and the
legacy BDB migration path), backup and recovery, rescanning, wallet RPCs,
and wallet-facing pieces of the GUI. Fee estimation is wallet when the
change is about how the wallet uses it.

Borderline: a descriptor or PSBT change that affects only `bitcoin-tx` or
RPC without wallet code is rpc, not wallet. An `interfaces::Wallet`
change is both wallet and ipc.

## What matters here

Fund safety first: anything that could lose keys, double-spend
unintentionally, create an unspendable output, or corrupt the wallet
database. Then backup, recovery, and migration correctness, including the
legacy-to-descriptor migration path that every remaining legacy user
must cross. Then privacy of transaction creation (address reuse, change
detection, fingerprinting). Then user-visible reliability: hangs, slow
rescans, confusing failures, wrong balances. Then features users have
asked for, with evidence they have asked.

The rubric does not ask whether Bitcoin Core should have a wallet. It
asks, given that it does, what a wallet user needs most.
